title: Making a pruning cut on a bush rose: removing a whole stem, or shortening one back to a bud

common.applies_to: Established Hybrid Tea, Floribunda or Grandiflora bush rose (a rose that has passed PKR-SGT-000003); dormant pruning
common.preserved_uncertainty: Distance above the bud (C2): most sources say about a quarter inch; a few say up to half an inch. Both are defensible answers to the same tradeoff (too close risks killing the bud; too far risks the stub dying back). All the quarter-inch sources are from the United States. Slant direction (C3): most sources say "away from the bud"; a few say "in the same direction as the bud", and it's unresolved whether that's the same technique. Whether angle and bud direction matter at all (C11): rose societies in South Australia and South Africa say they matter little, or recommend a straight cut; neither gives a reason. The approved default keeps the majority convention. Sealing (C4, AF-30, AF-35): most sources, including every UK and New Zealand source, don't mention it. Where rose sources recommend it, the reason is to keep cane-boring insects out of the soft pith, not to help the cut heal. General tree research finds that wound dressings don't help healing, which answers a different question. No trial of sealed against unsealed rose canes was found. Stubs (AF-29): five of the nine sources are about dead canes, so whether the rule applies equally to every kind of removal isn't directly addressed. Two kinds of cut (AF-31): only one of the three sources is rose-specific. Outward bud (AF-21): two sources allow an exception for a cane that already spreads sideways.

removeStem.text: Cut the stem off where it starts: at the base, at the bud union, or where it joins its parent stem. Don't leave a stub.

shorten.text: Cut just above a bud that faces outward, away from the centre of the bush.
Cut about a quarter of an inch (about 6 mm) above the bud. Up to half an inch is also fine if you'd rather avoid the stub dying back.
Make the cut on a slant, at roughly 45 degrees, not flat.
Slant the cut away from the bud.

seal.text: On cuts roughly pencil-thick or larger, you can seal the end with wood glue, nail polish or pruning sealer, to keep cane-boring insects out. Thinner cuts don't need it.
